storySpine.startingBelief: B.Com and BBA contain entirely different subjects.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student reviews degree brochures to choose an academic path.
storySpine.observation: Both programmes list 'Business Organization & Management' in Semester I.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: If titles match, the syllabus content might differ in depth.
storySpine.changedAction: Requesting syllabus breakdown from course offices.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Student writes specific email inquiry to department offices.
storySpine.channelExperience: Viewer sees an evidence-backed correction of a common degree-partitioning myth.

candidates.title: The Shared Title Check
candidates.audienceGap: Assumption that degree titles define exclusive subject sets.
candidates.viewerChange: Viewer learns to verify specific course lists rather than assuming degree exclusivity.
candidates.concept: Comparing two official programme documents for shared course titles.
candidates.payoff: Student stops guessing and starts asking for concrete syllabus depth.
candidates.hlni: Business Organization & Management appears in both JOY University B.Com (p.5) and BBA (p.9) documents for 2025-26 cohorts (https://joyuniversity.edu.in/).
candidates.support: Official JOY University PDFs for 2025-26 admissions.
candidates.interpretationRule: Title match is not content match; use it to trigger further inquiry.
candidates.visibleProof: Comparison of two official PDF document snapshots showing identical row content.
candidates.limitations: Only applies to the specific Semester I subject; does not imply identical depth or outcomes.

demonstration.input: Two official university PDF pages displayed side-by-side.
demonstration.observation: Both documents show the same course title.
demonstration.nextQuestion: What is the assessment difference for this shared subject?

storySpine.startingBelief: Choosing a degree is a final, all-or-nothing decision.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student wants to ensure their chosen path has the right support.
storySpine.observation: A list of tasks is provided without grading criteria.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Knowing the task is useless without knowing how it is evaluated.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Student fills a worksheet with specific assessment-related columns.
storySpine.channelExperience: Viewer learns a systematic method to evaluate any degree path.

candidates.title: The Evaluation Audit
candidates.audienceGap: Confusion between knowing a task and knowing its assessment standard.
candidates.viewerChange: Viewer shifts from degree-label browsing to assessment-method questioning.
candidates.concept: Using a three-column worksheet to distinguish tasks from assessment metrics.
candidates.payoff: Student gains a repeatable tool for evaluating any academic course.
candidates.hlni: A task label does not reveal what is assessed or how feedback is provided; treat these as distinct data points.
candidates.support: Logical separation of variables in academic assessment.
candidates.interpretationRule: If criteria are unknown, the degree decision is premature.
candidates.visibleProof: A filled-in three-column grid separating Task, Assessment, and Feedback.
candidates.limitations: Does not predict personal enjoyment or career success.

demonstration.input: Worksheet with 'Task Name' filled in as 'Business Report'.
demonstration.visibleInput: Task: Business Report. What is the grading criteria?
demonstration.observation: No information provided on rubric or feedback.
demonstration.nextQuestion: Is a marking rubric available for this assignment?

storySpine.startingBelief: I must choose the same degree as my friend to compare paths.
storySpine.studentSituation: Two friends feel lost comparing their degree choices.
storySpine.observation: Both identify a specific point where they don't know the course requirements.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: General worry doesn't solve the lack of specific course data.
storySpine.changedAction: Recording the specific gap for the next meeting.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Friends swap notes on what they actually need to ask the office.
storySpine.channelExperience: Viewer sees a supportive, practical way to navigate uncertainty.

candidates.title: The Friend-to-Friend Audit
candidates.audienceGap: Reliance on peer-group choices rather than individual investigation.
candidates.viewerChange: Viewer moves from seeking comfort to seeking specific answers.
candidates.concept: Using a journal to track specific questions about course tasks.
candidates.payoff: Both students leave with a clear action plan.
candidates.hlni: A journal of specific sticking points is more effective than comparing global degree labels.
candidates.support: Individualised inquiry replaces vague degree comparison.
candidates.interpretationRule: Specific questions generate better answers from administration.
candidates.visibleProof: Notebook entries showing specific questions about syllabus requirements.
candidates.limitations: Journaling does not measure aptitude or long-term engagement.

demonstration.input: A shared notebook page used during a study session.
demonstration.visibleInput: Task: Market Analysis. Sticking point: Data sources.
demonstration.observation: Neither knows the required data source standard.
demonstration.nextQuestion: What specific data sources are required for this analysis?

storySpine.startingBelief: If I can't decide, I must be missing the 'right' degree.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student feels overwhelmed by degree requirements.
storySpine.observation: The student lists preferences and finds gaps in verification.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Preferences are choices; requirements are mandatory constraints.
storySpine.changedAction: Checking actual requirements instead of assuming eligibility.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Student marks 'to-verify' next to a preferred course module.
storySpine.channelExperience: Viewer learns to distinguish personal desire from institutional fact.

candidates.title: The Preference Check
candidates.audienceGap: Assuming a preferred course is automatically an available one.
candidates.viewerChange: Viewer learns to verify prerequisites before deciding on a path.
candidates.concept: A two-column list separating 'Preferred' from 'Verified Requirements'.
candidates.payoff: Student prioritizes verified paths over assumed ones.
candidates.hlni: Preferences are not proof of availability; verify requirements before finalizing a choice.
candidates.support: Logical distinction between desire and factual constraint.
candidates.interpretationRule: Unknown requirements must be verified before the option is treated as valid.
candidates.limitations: Does not replace university admission eligibility checks.

demonstration.observation: Prerequisites are not listed or understood.
demonstration.nextQuestion: What are the specific prerequisites for this module?

storySpine.startingBelief: A task looks like it belongs to one degree based on its difficulty.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student tries to guess which degree a sample task comes from.
storySpine.observation: The task is missing its institutional source.
storySpine.focus: The impossibility of classification without data.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: The task lacks markers like a programme name or code.
storySpine.changedAction: Searching for the source instead of guessing.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Student labels the task 'Insufficient Info' and lists required source details.
storySpine.channelExperience: Viewer experiences the surprise of missing evidence.

candidates.title: The Unlabeled Task
candidates.audienceGap: Belief that tasks are inherently degree-specific.
candidates.viewerChange: Viewer learns to identify when information is missing.
candidates.concept: Presenting an unlabeled business task to expose the need for source data.
candidates.device: A visual puzzle where the source is hidden.
candidates.payoff: Student stops making unfounded assumptions about degree content.
candidates.hlni: Without a source linking a task to a programme, you cannot determine its origin.
candidates.visibleProof: The reveal of an 'Insufficient Information' label over the task.
candidates.limitations: Does not explain why some tasks might be shared.

demonstration.visibleInput: Task: Create a 5-year budget plan. Source: [MISSING]
demonstration.nextQuestion: Which specific course document contains this task?

storySpine.startingBelief: Similar-looking totals mean the underlying work is the same.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student compares two degree modules based on total credit hours.
storySpine.observation: The total credits are identical, but the component parts differ.
storySpine.focus: The importance of detail over aggregates.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Total numbers hide the actual mix of practical vs theoretical work.
storySpine.changedAction: Asking for a breakdown of component modules.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Student creates a bar chart showing the composition difference.
storySpine.channelExperience: Viewer sees how aggregate data can be misleading.

candidates.title: The Aggregate Reveal
candidates.audienceGap: Using totals to compare degrees without checking composition.
candidates.viewerChange: Viewer learns to inspect component parts of academic loads.
candidates.concept: Displaying two credit loads with equal totals but different content.
candidates.payoff: Student avoids making degree comparisons based on surface-level totals.
candidates.hlni: The same aggregate total can be composed of different components; always ask for the breakdown.
candidates.interpretationRule: Aggregates are insufficient for comparing course focus.
candidates.limitations: Does not prove which composition is 'better'.

demonstration.visibleInput: Module A: 5 theory, 5 practice. Module B: 2 theory, 8 practice.
demonstration.observation: Totals are the same but composition is clearly different.
demonstration.nextQuestion: What is the detailed breakdown of the module components?

plan.contrast: Trust focuses on verifiable curriculum documents, Connection uses peer-based task journaling for personal clarity, and Discovery uses the 'insufficient information' logic to challenge assumptions about task origin.

issues: integrity: In concept 'conn_01', the story spine's 'whyQuestionFollows' claims 'General worry doesn't solve the lack of specific course data', but the 'changedAction' is recording the gap, and the 'visibleConsequence' is swapping notes; these do not demonstrate a direct, logical evolution from a question to an improved decision. Correction: Define a specific, concrete question the student asks the course office based on the recorded gap that visibly improves their understanding of course requirements.

integrity: In concept 'disc_01', the 'nextQuestion' listed in the demonstration ('Which specific course document contains this task?') does not follow from the 'observation' that there is insufficient information; the question should be the changed action that addresses the lack of information. Correction: Update the 'nextQuestion' to reflect an actionable step the student takes to find the missing source or contact the correct department.

plan.contrast: Trust uses official document evidence to correct title myths; Connection uses peer-led journaling to turn confusion into specific inquiries; Discovery uses the 'insufficient information' logic to expose why tasks cannot be classified without sources.

issues: insight: The connection between classifying an expense and auditing a budget is a non-sequitur in the instructions for the 'Unlabeled Task' concept, contradicting the core requirement that concepts must maintain academic coherence. Correction: Ensure the 'Unlabeled Task' concept uses a business-related task that aligns with the B.Com and BBA curricula mentioned, such as a financial reporting task, instead of an unrelated budgeting example.
